summary: This Standards Track document defines SCIM security events using Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417), so SCIM service providers and receivers can exchange messages asynchronously. It updates RFC 7643 with extra ServiceProviderConfig attributes and RFC 7644 with an optional new capability.

plainLanguage.summary: SCIM is a protocol for changing user and group records in identity systems. This RFC lets a service provider send a token whenever a record changes, so other systems learn about the change without asking for it. The token names the record and either carries its new values or only lists which attributes changed.

questions: what is a scim security event
how do asynchronous scim requests work
subtitle: How SCIM services push change notices as Security Event Tokens instead of being polled.

tldr.problem: SCIM clients change user and group records over HTTP. When many independent clients do this, each one ends up with an old copy, and fetching updates with repeated GET requests becomes costly as the number of changes and resources grows.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SCIM events carried in Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417). Each token names the resource that changed and either carries its new values or only the list of changed attributes. It adds a Prefer: respond-async request, a Set-Txn response header, and a securityEvents discovery attribute.
tldr.outcome: Receivers learn about changes without asking for them and decide their own follow-up action. The RFC updates RFC 7643 and RFC 7644 and creates an IANA registry of SCIM event URIs.

today: RFC 9967 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It updates RFC 7643 with new ServiceProviderConfig attributes and RFC 7644 with an optional asynchronous request capability. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SCIM Needs Events
sections.content:
SCIM clients issue commands to a SCIM service provider over HTTP, using methods such as POST, PATCH and DELETE, and each command changes the state of a SCIM resource. When several independent clients change resources, individual clients fall out of date as those changes occur.

The alternative is polling: the client sends periodic SCIM GET requests to find out what changed. The RFC says this rapidly becomes problematic as the number of changes and the number of resources increases.

Instead, the RFC defines Security Events shared over an established event feed, a logical series of events shared with a unique receiving client. A Security Event Token (SET) is defined in RFC 8417. A SET conveys information about a state change that has occurred at a SCIM service provider.

A SET is not a command. Each Event Receiver determines the best local follow-up action within its own context, for example reconciling schema and resource type differences between domains. The RFC defines three kinds of SCIM Security Event: asynchronous request completion, resource replication, and provisioning coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: Many programs change user and group records through one service. Each program then holds an old copy of the data. Instead of asking for updates all the time, the service can send a short token when a record changes. The token is a notice, not an instruction, so the receiving system decides what to do next.

sections.title: Identifying the Subject and Common Attributes
sections.content:
A SCIM Event is a SET whose events claim contains one or more event URI subclaims, each a JSON object holding the event information. The RFC defines the URI prefix urn:ietf:params:scim:event and groups events into the feed and prov sub-namespaces, with a misc class for asynchronous completion.

Events MUST use the sub_id claim from RFC 9493 to identify the subject. It MUST sit in the main JWT claims body and MUST NOT sit inside an event payload. The JWT sub claim MUST NOT be used, to prevent confusion with authorization tokens.

The sub_id object carries a format of scim and a required uri, the relative path of the resource, such as /Users/2b2f880af6674ac284bae9381673d462. It may also carry externalId and id. When those are not enough to match a resource across domains, the object MAY carry attributes whose SCIM uniqueness is server or global, such as emails or userName.

Three attributes apply to every event. txn is a string identifying a transaction at the service provider; unlike the per-token jti, it stays the same across retransmission and across publication to multiple receivers, so a receiver can detect duplicates. version is the ETag version of the resource. Only one of data or attributes is provided, never both.
sections.plainLanguage: Each token says which record changed by giving its path on the service, such as /Users/2b2f880af6674ac284bae9381673d462. It also carries a transaction number that stays the same when one change is sent to several receivers or sent again, so a receiver can tell a duplicate from a new change.

sections.title: Feed and Provisioning Events
sections.content:
Feed events use the prefix urn:ietf:params:scim:event:feed. feed:add says the resource has been added to the event feed. It does not mean the resource is new: the RFC's example is an existing user who was given a new role, which caused the resource to join a feed. feed:remove says the resource has left the feed, and does not mean the resource was deleted or deactivated.

Provisioning events use the prefix urn:ietf:params:scim:event:prov and describe resource changes inside a SCIM service provider. When the data payload attribute is included, the event URI MUST end with full; otherwise it ends with notice. In full mode the data attribute holds the final representation of the resource as the service provider would return it. In notice mode the attributes attribute lists the attributes created or modified, for example userName, emails and name.familyName. Exactly one of the two payload attributes MUST be present, and they MUST NOT both be present.

The provisioning event types are prov:create, prov:patch and prov:put, each in a full or notice form, plus prov:delete, prov:activate and prov:deactivate. A delete event has no payload attributes, so the qualifiers full and notice are not used, and no feed:remove is issued alongside a delete. The id assigned by the service provider is shared in a create event, so that all replicas in a domain may use the same resource identifier.

An activate event does not necessarily reflect a state change at the provider. It may only mean that the account is ready for use, as agreed between publisher and receiver; the RFC notes that an activated resource can represent an account that may be logged in. A deactivate event means the resource has been deactivated and disabled, and the exact meaning SHOULD be agreed between the two parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of event describe a change. A full event carries the record as it now stands. A notice event carries only the names of the attributes that changed, and the receiver can then fetch the values. A delete event carries nothing at all.

sections.title: Asynchronous Requests and the Set-Txn Header
sections.content:
A SCIM client MAY ask for asynchronous processing by sending a normal POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE with the HTTP Prefer header set to respond-async, as defined in RFC 7240. The RFC gives the reason: to avoid holding HTTP connections open during long requests when the result is not needed by the client, or when the result is delivered to another entity. The Accept header MUST be ignored for an asynchronous response, and the wait preference SHOULD be supported to set a maximum time before the provider MAY choose to answer asynchronously.

The provider then returns either a normal SCIM response or HTTP status code 202 (Accepted). The asynchronous response MUST contain no response body. It carries the new Set-Txn header, whose value MUST match the txn claim in the later Security Event Token, plus the Preference-Applied header from RFC 7240 and a Location header. That Location value MUST be either a URI where the completion token may be retrieved with an HTTP GET, or the normal SCIM location header response from RFC 7644.

The Set-Txn header field is defined in Section 3 of the RFC. It MUST be used in SCIM responses that return 202 with no message body. Its value is a unique string, for example a Globally Unique Identifier, which the client uses to find the matching SET. Intermediaries SHOULD NOT insert, modify or delete the value, and clients MAY ignore it when confirmation of completion is not required.

For a SCIM bulk request handled asynchronously, one Asynchronous Request Completion Event MUST be generated for each requested operation: a bulk request with 10 operations produces 10 completion events. The txn claim of each event is the value originally returned to the client, followed by a colon and the zero-based index of the operation in the original bulk request, for example 2d80e537a3f64622b0347b641ebc8f44:0 and 2d80e537a3f64622b0347b641ebc8f44:1. The bulkId parameter MUST NOT be used for this, because it is temporary and is not present on every operation.

The completion event is urn:ietf:params:scim:event:misc:asyncresp. Its payload is the same as a single SCIM Bulk Response Operation and carries the method, the version and the status. If an error occurs during asynchronous processing, the event operation MUST include a response attribute holding a non-200-series HTTP status and the sub-attributes defined in Section 3.12 of RFC 7644.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask for an answer later by adding Prefer: respond-async to a request. The provider replies with status 202 and a Set-Txn header, and no body. Later a completion token arrives carrying the same transaction number, the HTTP method used, and the status code of the original request.

sections.title: Discovering Event Support
sections.content:
The RFC adds an optional complex attribute named securityEvents to the urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:ServiceProviderConfig schema defined in Section 5 of RFC 7643. The attribute is OPTIONAL, and when it is absent it indicates that the SCIM service provider does not support, or is not currently configured for, Security Events.

Its first sub-attribute, asyncRequest, is a case-insensitive string with three values. none indicates that the asynchronous requests of Section 2.5.1.1 are not supported. long indicates that the server completes requests asynchronously at its own discretion, for example based on a maximum wait time. request indicates that the server completes requests asynchronously when the client asks for it.

The second sub-attribute, eventUris, is a multivalued string listing the SET event URIs the server is capable of generating and delivering through a SET stream, using the push-based or poll-based delivery mechanisms of RFC 8935 and RFC 8936. The RFC states that this information is informational only, and that stream registration and configuration are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider advertises what it can do in an optional securityEvents part of its service configuration. The asyncRequest value says whether asynchronous requests are refused, done at the provider's discretion, or done only on request. The eventUris value lists the event types the provider can deliver.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The security and privacy considerations of RFC 8417, RFC 8935 and RFC 8936 also apply here.

SETs may contain sensitive information, including personally identifiable information. In that case, SET transmitters and SET recipients MUST protect the confidentiality of the SET contents in transit using TLS. Event Publishers can keep events available for longer than the usual retry window, and Event Receivers MUST ensure events are persisted, directly or indirectly, before acknowledging receipt, to meet local recovery needs. Access to event recovery and forwarding MUST be limited to the parties needed to support recovery or forwarding.

When the Event Publisher is not communicating directly with the Event Receiver, an attacker or other system may insert an event. Event Receivers MUST therefore verify the originator of a SET using JSON Web Signature signatures from RFC 7515. The RFC adds that validating signatures helps auditing, because signed SETs are protected from tampering if an intermediate system, such as a TLS-terminating proxy, decrypts the payload before sending it on.

Some SCIM resources change often. A group with more than a few thousand member values can produce excessive change rates and a loss of events. The RFC recommends using SCIM PATCH rather than SCIM PUT for large groups, or using the put notice event as a trigger to fetch the full information later, or combining the patch notice event with periodic GETs, or aggregating several membership changes into a single event.

For asynchronous requests, the provider returns a URI for retrieving the event result. An unauthorized party could obtain completion information by querying that endpoint, so the returned URI endpoint MUST be protected and requires an HTTP Authorization header or some other form of client authentication. For privacy, the RFC assumes either a common administrative domain with one owner of the data, or a cooperative relationship where information is shared on an as-authorized and as-needed basis.
sections.plainLanguage: Tokens can contain personal data, so they must travel over TLS. A receiver must store an event before it acknowledges it, and must check the signature when the publisher does not send the token directly. The address given for an asynchronous result must require authentication.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the HTTP field name Set-Txn in the HTTP Field Name Registry, with the status permanent and Section 3 of RFC 9967 as the reference.

It also adds a reference to Section 4 of the document to the urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:ServiceProviderConfig entry in the SCIM Server-Related Schema URIs registry.

Finally, IANA created a new registry called "SCIM Event URIs" under the SCIM Schema URIs registry group. The registration procedure is Expert Review, and new registrations are evaluated by designated experts for relevance to SCIM-based systems and to avoid duplication or conflict with event definitions outside SCIM. The sub-namespace ID assigned is "event", and the Namespace Specific String of every URN in it follows the structure urn:ietf:params:scim:event:{class}:{name}:{other}. The class is one of feed, prov or misc; the name is a descriptive event name such as create; and the other part is an optional qualifier such as full or notice.

The initial contents of the registry hold the eleven event URIs defined by the document: the two feed events, the create, patch and put events in both notice and full forms, the delete, activate and deactivate events, and the asynchronous response event.
sections.plainLanguage: The new header name and the event names are registered so that every implementation uses the same spelling for them. The registry is reviewed by experts, and a name that has been allocated is never reused for a different meaning.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use the Events (Appendix A)
sections.content:
Appendix A describes two non-normative ways of using SCIM events.

In Domain-Based Replication (DBR), the objective is to synchronize resource changes between SCIM service providers in a common administrative domain. Complete information about modified resources is shared between replicas for immediate processing, so the events usually use the full form with the data payload attribute, and no callback is needed. The RFC assumes that servers sharing DBR events are secured by a common access policy and that all servers are required to be up to date.

In Coordinated Provisioning (CP), the events act as change notification without raw data. The receiver of an event must call back to the originating SCIM service provider, for example with a SCIM GET request, to reconcile the newly changed resource. An event feed can be limited to a subset of resources, such as users who have consented to sharing information between domains.

The RFC lists the benefits of CP: differences in schema between domains, such as a receiving domain that may only be interested in or allowed to access a few attributes; different receivers with different access rights, which allows data filtering; receivers taking independent action, such as choosing which domain to prefer in a conflict; and throttling or buffering, for example marking resources as dirty on receipt and fetching them on a schedule. The stated disadvantage is cost: each event received might trigger a callback, and that cost should be weighed against producing filtered information in each event for each receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: In Domain-Based Replication the event carries the whole record, so a replica can store it without asking. In Coordinated Provisioning the event only says that something changed, and the receiver fetches the record if it needs it. That costs a request per event, but it lets each receiver fetch only what it is allowed to see.
